content: Acute respiratory infections, particularly pneumonia, are the leading cause of death in children under five years of age in low-income countries. Some clinical trials have suggested that vitamin A supplementation can reduce the severity of respiratory infections and mortality in children with measles. This study aimed to evaluate whether vitamin A supplementation is effective as an adjunctive treatment in children diagnosed with non-measles pneumonia. The researchers conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, CINAHL, Biological Abstracts, Current Contents, and the Chinese Biomedicine Database, covering studies published up to mid-2010. They included only parallel-arm randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving children under 15 years of age with non-measles pneumonia who were treated with adjunctive vitamin A. Data from six trials involving a total of 1,740 children were analyzed. The results showed no significant reduction in mortality associated with pneumonia in children treated with vitamin A compared to those who were not (pooled odds ratio [OR] 1.29; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.63 to 2.66). Additionally, there was no statistically significant difference in the duration of hospital stay between the two groups (mean difference [MD] 0.08; 95% CI -0.43 to 0.59). Interestingly, the severity of disease appeared to worsen in children who received high-dose vitamin A supplementation compared to those who received a placebo. However, low-dose vitamin A supplementation significantly reduced the recurrence rate of bronchopneumonia (OR 0.12; 95% CI 0.03 to 0.46). Furthermore, moderate doses of vitamin A were associated with a significant reduction in the time to remission of clinical signs in children with normal serum retinol levels (> 200 µg/L). The authors concluded that the evidence does not support a significant reduction in mortality, morbidity, or the clinical course of pneumonia with adjunctive vitamin A treatment in children with non-measles pneumonia. However, it is important to note that not all studies measured all relevant outcomes, which limited the number of studies that could be included in the meta-analyses. This limitation may have reduced the statistical power to detect significant differences.
